title: PLATE: Plasticity-Tunable Efficient Adapters for Geometry-Aware Continual Learning
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: Standard adaptation methods cause large functional drift on old-task data; our constrained update confines change to the new task's region.
layout: 3 panels side-by-side, left-to-right, shared heatmap colorbar at right
description: Three side-by-side 2-D scatter panels on a two-moons-style binary classification toy problem, titled Full Finetuning, LoRA Finetuning and PLATE Finetuning. Each title lists forgetting on Dataset 1 (21.8%, 18.6%, 1.0%) and accuracy on Dataset 2 (100%, 100%, 99%). Dark blue points are the old task (D1) and orange-yellow points are the new task (D2). Teal and yellow curves mark the D1 and D2 decision boundaries. The background heatmap, from navy to bright yellow, shows how much the input Jacobian changed. Full fine-tuning and especially LoRA are yellow over the old-data region, with LoRA almost solid yellow on the left. PLATE stays dark blue around the old points and turns yellow only near the new data. A vertical colorbar on the right gives the scale, 0 to 60.
caption: Local-geometry view of forgetting on a continual learning 2-dimensional binary classification problem: Blue points denote the old-task dataset P0 and yellow points the new-task dataset P1; decision boundaries are shown when trained on P0 (blue curve) and after training on P1 (yellow curve). The background heatmap visualizes how training on P1 changes the model’s local input-output linearization, ∆(x) := ∥Jx(θ1, x) −Jx(θ0, x)∥F , where Jx(θ, x) := ∇xfθ(x) denotes the input Jacobian; this is distinct from the parameter Jacobian Jθ(x) := ∇θfθ(x) used throughout Sections 2.2–3.2. Retention is compromised when the heatmap turns yellow around the blue points (large drift on supp(P0)), while effective learning requires yellow regions around the yellow points (large drift concentrated near supp(P1)). This motivates our goal: parameter-efficient continual updates that localize drift away from the (often unavailable) old distribution while remaining expressive on the new task. (Left) Full fine-tuning induces large changes throughout, including on supp(P0), and the old boundary drifts. (Middle) LoRA restricts the parameter update but still produces substantial change on supp(P0). (Right) PLATE updates keep ∆(x) small on supp(P0) while permitting large changes near P1, concentrating plasticity where it is needed and preserving old behavior (see Figure 18 for PLATE hyperparameters sweep).
abstract: We develop a continual learning method for pretrained models that \emph{requires no access to old-task data}, addressing a practical barrier in foundation model adaptation where pretraining distributions are often unavailable. Our key observation is that pretrained networks exhibit substantial \emph{geometric redundancy}, and that this redundancy can be exploited in two complementary ways. First, redundant neurons provide a proxy for dominant pretraining-era feature directions, enabling the construction of approximately protected update subspaces directly from pretrained weights. Second, redundancy offers a natural bias for \emph{where} to place plasticity: by restricting updates to a subset of redundant neurons and constraining the remaining degrees of freedom, we obtain update families with reduced functional drift on the old-data distribution and improved worst-case retention guarantees. These insights lead to \textsc{PLATE} (\textbf{Pla}sticity-\textbf{T}unable \textbf{E}fficient Adapters), a continual learning method requiring no past-task data that provides explicit control over the plasticity-retention trade-off. PLATE parameterizes each layer with a structured low-rank update $ÎW = B A Q^\top$, where $B$ and $Q$ are computed once from pretrained weights and kept frozen, and only $A$ is trained on the new task. The code is available at https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/PLATE.
